### 4.2.3 Seasonality {#s4-2-3 .unnumbered .unlisted}

VAT followed a clear yearly pattern (Figure 4.4). The typical December was about 20% above the yearly average, and the typical February was about 15% below it. January and March were also below average, while October and November were slightly above. The decomposition in Figure 4.5 showed the same thing: a rising trend, a seasonal pattern that repeated every year with its peak in December, and a remainder that was small in most years but large in 2020 and in 2023–2024. These patterns explain why the predictors included a December indicator, the sine and cosine of the month, and the VAT change 12 months earlier.

![**Figure 4.4.** Seasonality of Domestic VAT: each month's VAT as a ratio of its calendar-year average. Values above the dashed line (1.00) are above-average months. Each box covers the middle half of the years.](figs/fig4_4.png){#fig-4-4 width=100%}

![**Figure 4.5.** Decomposition of log(VAT) into trend, seasonal and remainder parts.](figs/fig4_5.png){#fig-4-5 width=100%}

### 4.2.4 Unusual months {#s4-2-4 .unnumbered .unlisted}

Three months were flagged as unusual (Figure 4.6 and Table 4.2). All three were sharp rises: 75.3% in April 2020, 66.6% in November 2023 and 53.0% in August 2024. Each was followed by a fall. The August 2024 jump fell in the test period. These months were kept in the data (Chapter 3). They probably reflected real events or the timing of payments, but the data could not tell which. They mattered later, because no model could foresee a jump of this size.

| Month | VAT (GHS million) | Change (%) | z-score |
|:---------------|-----------------:|-----------:|---------:|

| August 2024 | 2,023 | 53.0 | 3.40 |

![**Figure 4.6.** Month-to-month percentage change in Domestic VAT. Red points mark the three months that are more than three standard deviations from the average change.](figs/fig4_6.png){#fig-4-6 width=100%}

### 4.2.5 Relationship between the predictors and the change in VAT {#s4-2-5 .unnumbered .unlisted}

Figure 4.7 shows the correlation between the change in log VAT (dVAT) and the predictors. The strongest link was with last month's VAT change (VAT_l1, −0.37): a large rise tended to be followed by a fall, and the opposite. The December indicator (0.26) and the VAT change 12 months earlier (0.22) had a positive link. The change in CIEA (0.16) and in the exchange rate (0.15) one month earlier had weaker positive links. Inflation and the T-bill rate had almost none. The predictors were not strongly correlated with each other, apart from the calendar variables and some VAT lags, so repeated information was not a serious problem.

No single predictor was strongly related to the change in VAT. This showed that the forecasting task was hard.

![**Figure 4.7.** Correlation between the monthly change in log VAT (dVAT) and the predictors.](figs/fig4_7.png){#fig-4-7 width=100%}

### 4.2.6 Stationarity of the series {#s4-2-6 .unnumbered .unlisted}

Table 4.3 reports the ADF and KPSS tests. The ADF test has a unit root (a series that keeps drifting) as its null hypothesis, so a small p-value points to a stable series. The KPSS test has stability as its null, so a large p-value points to a stable series. The raw VAT series and log VAT failed both tests: the ADF p-values were 0.990 and 0.268, and the KPSS p-value was at its lowest reported value of 0.01. The monthly change in log VAT passed both tests (ADF 0.01, KPSS 0.10), and so did the monthly changes in log FX, the T-bill rate and log CIEA. This supported the decision to forecast the monthly change in VAT rather than its level, and to enter the exchange rate, T-bill rate and CIEA as monthly changes. Inflation is already a monthly rate and was not tested.

: **Table 4.3.** Stationarity tests (p-values) `\label{tbl-4-3}`{=latex}

| Series | ADF p-value | KPSS p-value |
|:------------------------------------------|----------:|----------:|
| VAT (raw level) | 0.990 | 0.01 |
| log(VAT) | 0.268 | 0.01 |
| Change in log(VAT) (used in this study) | 0.01 | 0.10 |
| Change in log(FX) | 0.01 | 0.10 |
| Change in T-bill rate | 0.01 | 0.10 |
| Change in log(CIEA) | 0.01 | 0.10 |

*Note:* The p-values are reported at the limits of the test tables (ADF: smallest value 0.01; KPSS: between 0.01 and 0.10).

## 4.3 Training and Test Data {#s4-3 .unnumbered .unlisted}

Figure 4.8 shows the split. The test period was a demanding one. VAT in the 24 test months ranged from about GHS 1,150 million to GHS 2,070 million, which was higher than in most of the training period, and the period included the sharp jump of August 2024.

![**Figure 4.8.** Training period (up to December 2023) and test period (January 2024 to December 2025, shaded).](figs/fig4_8.png){#fig-4-8 width=100%}

## 4.4 Results of the Individual Models {#s4-4 .unnumbered .unlisted}

This section reports the results of applying the four machine learning models and the ARIMAX benchmark (Objective 1). Table 4.4 summarises the settings chosen for each model and, where available, the average validation RMSE on the log change in VAT. The validation errors of LASSO (about 0.134) and SVR (0.135) were lower than that of XGBoost (0.145), which already suggested that the simpler and kernel-based models suited this small sample better than the tree ensemble.

: **Table 4.4.** Settings chosen by rolling validation `\label{tbl-4-4}`{=latex}

| Model | Chosen setting | Validation RMSE |
|:-----------|:----------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------:|
| ARIMAX | Regression with ARIMA(0,0,1) errors; eight lagged predictors; no seasonal terms | – |
| LASSO | $\lambda$ = 0.00291 | about 0.134 |
| SVR | cost = 10, gamma = 0.005, epsilon = 0.1 | 0.135 |
| XGBoost | depth = 2, eta = 0.03, 300 trees, min child weight = 1, lambda = 1, alpha = 0.1, gamma = 0 | 0.145 |
| 1D-CNN | Fixed design; stopped early by the validation loss; five runs averaged | – |

### 4.4.1 ARIMAX {#s4-4-1 .unnumbered .unlisted}

The automatic search chose a regression model with ARIMA(0,0,1) errors. No seasonal terms were needed, because the seasonal pattern was already carried by the 12-month VAT lag and the December indicator. The residual checks in Figure 4.9 looked acceptable. The residuals moved around zero, almost all autocorrelations were inside the dashed limits (one lag, at about 7, was slightly outside), and the histogram was close to a normal curve. A few large residuals appeared in 2020 and in late 2023, which were the unusual months. The model was therefore a reasonable benchmark. The Ljung–Box test on the residuals (24 lags) gave $Q^{*} = 24.39$ with 23 degrees of freedom and a p-value of 0.383, so there was no evidence of autocorrelation left in the residuals.

Table 4.5 gives the estimated coefficients. The change in CIEA one month earlier (1.20) and the change in the exchange rate one month earlier (0.77) were the only regressors more than three standard errors from zero, and both were positive. The T-bill and inflation coefficients were close to zero, and the moving-average term was negative (−0.78), which fitted the tendency of VAT growth to fall back after a strong month. These findings agreed with those of LASSO.

: **Table 4.5.** ARIMAX estimates (regression with ARIMA(0,0,1) errors, training period) `\label{tbl-4-5}`{=latex}

| Term | Coefficient | Standard error |
|:----------------|-----------:|-----------:|
| MA(1) | −0.7823 | 0.1483 |
| FX, lag 1 | 0.7669 | 0.2299 |
| FX, lag 2 | −0.4252 | 0.2461 |
| T-bill, lag 1 | −0.0004 | 0.0062 |
| T-bill, lag 2 | 0.0022 | 0.0061 |
| CIEA, lag 1 | 1.2036 | 0.3072 |
| CIEA, lag 2 | −0.1570 | 0.3182 |
| Inflation, lag 1 | 0.0010 | 0.0088 |
| Inflation, lag 2 | 0.0063 | 0.0078 |

*Note:* $\sigma^{2} = 0.01322$; log likelihood = 119.5; AIC = −218.99; AICc = −217.47; BIC = −188.56.

![**Figure 4.9.** Residual checks for the ARIMAX model: residuals over time (top), autocorrelation function (bottom left) and histogram of the residuals (bottom right).](figs/fig4_9.png){#fig-4-9 width=100%}

### 4.4.2 LASSO {#s4-4-2 .unnumbered .unlisted}

The validation error was lowest when $\lambda$ was 0.00291 (Figure 4.10), with a validation RMSE of about 0.134 (in units of log change). The error rose quickly for larger $\lambda$.

![**Figure 4.10.** LASSO tuning: average validation RMSE for each value of lambda. The dashed line marks the chosen value.](figs/fig4_10.png){#fig-4-10 width=100%}

Figure 4.11 shows which predictors LASSO kept. The positive coefficients were for the change in CIEA one and two months earlier, the change in the exchange rate one month earlier, the December indicator and the VAT change 12 months earlier. The negative coefficients were for VAT changes one, two and three months earlier. Inflation, the second lag of the exchange rate, the second lag of the T-bill rate and the cosine of the month were removed. The T-bill rate lag 1 and the sine of the month were almost zero. Predictors are measured in different units, so the sizes of the bars should not be compared too closely.

In plain terms, VAT growth tended to fall back after a strong month, tended to be higher in December and in the same month as last year, and was higher after months of stronger economic activity and a rising exchange rate (a weaker cedi). These are associations, not proof of cause.

![**Figure 4.11.** LASSO coefficients at the chosen lambda. Predictors with no bar were set to zero.](figs/fig4_11.png){#fig-4-11 width=100%}

### 4.4.3 SVR {#s4-4-3 .unnumbered .unlisted}

Figure 4.12 shows the SVR tuning results. The best setting was a moderate cost (about 10) with a small gamma (0.005) and epsilon 0.1, with a validation RMSE of about 0.135. Very high cost (100) was clearly worse, with errors up to about 0.18. This suggested overfitting when the model followed the training data too closely. A large gamma (0.2) was also worse.

![**Figure 4.12.** SVR tuning: average validation RMSE for each combination of cost and gamma, for two values of epsilon. Lighter cells mean lower error.](figs/fig4_12.png){#fig-4-12 width=100%}

### 4.4.4 XGBoost {#s4-4-4 .unnumbered .unlisted}

Figure 4.13 shows that the VAT change of the previous month carried about one third of the total importance. It was followed by the change in CIEA one month earlier (about 10%), the VAT changes two and three months earlier, the exchange rate two months earlier and the cosine of the month. This agreed with LASSO: the recent VAT changes and economic activity mattered most, while inflation and the T-bill rate mattered little. The best setting found by the random search used shallow trees (depth 2), a low learning rate (0.03) and 300 trees, which again pointed to a model that needed to be kept simple in a small sample. Its validation RMSE (0.145) was higher than those of LASSO and SVR.

![**Figure 4.13.** XGBoost: importance (gain) of each predictor.](figs/fig4_13.png){#fig-4-13 width=100%}

### 4.4.5 1D-CNN {#s4-4-5 .unnumbered .unlisted}

Figure 4.14 shows the learning curve of the first of the five runs. The training loss fell steadily, but the validation loss was lowest at the second epoch and then rose. Training stopped at epoch 22 and the weights from the second epoch were restored. This meant that the network began to overfit almost at once. The validation loss also stayed above the training loss throughout. The validation months (about 2022–2023) were more volatile than earlier years, but the pattern still showed that 155 training months were too few for the network to learn much.

![**Figure 4.14.** 1D-CNN learning curve for the first of the five training runs: training and validation loss (mean squared error on scaled data).](figs/fig4_14.png){#fig-4-14 width=100%}

## 4.5 Forecast Performance on the Test Data {#s4-5 .unnumbered .unlisted}

### 4.5.1 Accuracy measures {#s4-5-1 .unnumbered .unlisted}

This section compares the machine learning models with the conventional benchmarks (Objective 2). Table 4.6 gives the test results for the 24 months from January 2024 to December 2025, Table 4.7 gives the rank of each model on each measure, and Figure 4.15 shows the errors as bars.

The main points were as follows.

- **SVR was the best model on all three measures.** Its RMSE was GHS 201.40 million, which was 16.0% lower than the Naive forecast. Its MAPE was 9.36%.
- **The lead of SVR over ARIMAX was small.** The RMSE differed by about 0.3%, the MAE by about 4% and the MAPE by about 2%.
- **LASSO and XGBoost beat the Naive forecast on RMSE (by 14.6% and 12.3%) but not ARIMAX.** On MAPE, both were slightly worse than the Naive forecast, and LASSO was also slightly worse on MAE.
- **The 1D-CNN had the same RMSE as the Naive forecast.** Its MAE and MAPE were a little better than Naive. Its MAE was also slightly lower than that of ARIMAX, but its RMSE and MAPE were worse.
- **The Seasonal Naive forecast was far the worst.** VAT grows over time, so the value of the same month last year was usually too low.

| Model | RMSE | MAE | MAPE (%) | RMSE gain over Naive (%) |
|:---------------|-------:|-------:|---------:|-----------------------:|
| SVR | 201.40 | 145.59 | 9.36 | 16.0 |
| ARIMAX | 201.94 | 152.16 | 9.52 | 15.7 |
| LASSO | 204.69 | 158.09 | 10.02 | 14.6 |
| XGBoost | 210.25 | 155.78 | 10.07 | 12.3 |
| 1D-CNN | 239.63 | 151.21 | 9.65 | 0.0 |
| Naive | 239.65 | 156.44 | 9.82 | 0.0 |
| Seasonal Naive | 371.59 | 329.89 | 20.43 | −55.1 |

| Model | RMSE | MAE | MAPE |
|:---------------|-----:|-----:|-----:|
| SVR | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| ARIMAX | 2 | 3 | 2 |
| LASSO | 3 | 6 | 5 |
| XGBoost | 4 | 4 | 6 |
| 1D-CNN | 5 | 2 | 3 |
| Naive | 6 | 5 | 4 |
| Seasonal Naive | 7 | 7 | 7 |

All typical errors were large. The best model was wrong by about 9% in an average month, or about GHS 146 million.

![**Figure 4.15.** Test-set errors of the seven models: MAE, MAPE and RMSE (lower is better).](figs/fig4_15.png){#fig-4-15 width=100%}

### 4.5.2 Forecasts and errors over time {#s4-5-2 .unnumbered .unlisted}

Figure 4.16 shows the forecasts against the actual values. All models followed the general upward movement and the usual month-to-month changes, but none predicted the sharp jump of August 2024, when VAT rose to about GHS 2,020 million. The errors in that month were between about GHS 520 million (ARIMAX) and GHS 700 million (Naive) (Figure 4.18). In the next month, VAT fell back to about GHS 1,390 million. The Naive forecast and the 1D-CNN repeated the August spike and missed by about GHS 640 million and GHS 690 million, while the other models missed by less than GHS 270 million. All models except the Seasonal Naive also over-forecast January 2024, when VAT dropped to about GHS 1,240 million, by GHS 280 million to GHS 470 million.

Most of the large errors fell in the same few months for all models. This meant that the models differed little because the biggest misses came from shocks that none of them could predict. A single month such as August 2024 had a large effect on RMSE, which is why the RMSE values of the top four models were so close.

Figure 4.17 shows predicted against actual values. The SVR and XGBoost points lay closer to the dashed line than the others for mid-range values. The ARIMAX forecasts stayed within a narrow band and reacted less to high and low months. All models under-forecast the highest months. The Seasonal Naive forecasts lay mostly below the line, which agreed with the positive errors in Figure 4.18.

![**Figure 4.16.** Actual and predicted Domestic VAT in the test period (GHS million). All forecasts are one step ahead.](figs/fig4_16.png){#fig-4-16 width=100%}

![**Figure 4.17.** Predicted against actual Domestic VAT for each model in the test period. The dashed line marks perfect forecasts.](figs/fig4_17.png){#fig-4-17 width=100%}

![**Figure 4.18.** Forecast errors over time (actual minus predicted, GHS million). Positive values mean the model forecast too little.](figs/fig4_18.png){#fig-4-18 width=100%}

## 4.6 Discussion {#s4-6 .unnumbered .unlisted}

This section discusses the results in relation to the three research questions in Section 1.5. Each research question matched one of the three objectives in Section 1.4, and each answer is compared with the earlier studies reviewed in Chapter 2.

### 4.6.1 Accuracy of the Machine Learning Models {#s4-6-1 .unnumbered .unlisted}

This section answers Research Question 1 and meets Objective 1. All four machine learning models were applied successfully and produced one-month-ahead forecasts of Domestic VAT. On the test data, their MAPE was between 9.4% and 10.1%, which means that a typical forecast was wrong by about one-tenth. The RMSE was between 201 and 210 (GHS million) for SVR, LASSO and XGBoost, and 240 for the 1D-CNN, which was the same as the Naive forecast. Compared with the Naive forecast, SVR, LASSO and XGBoost reduced the RMSE by 12% to 16%. The models therefore gave a useful forecast, but the average error was still large.

These results are more modest than the accuracy above 98% reported for a multivariate LSTM model in Nigeria (Ajisola, 2023). The two studies used different data, forecast periods and accuracy measures, so the figures cannot be compared directly. The present results are closer to studies that found that machine learning does not always give large gains when data are limited (Jayanti et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2025). The weak result of the 1D-CNN also fits what was said in Section 2.3.3: models that need more data, such as neural networks, find it hard to learn from fewer than 200 monthly observations. The study also adds to the work of Ofori et al. (2021), who used only time-series methods for VAT in Ghana, by showing that machine learning models can be applied to Domestic VAT and can match, and slightly improve on, a well-specified ARIMAX model.

### 4.6.2 The Most Accurate Forecasting Model {#s4-6-2 .unnumbered .unlisted}

This section answers Research Question 2 and meets Objective 2. SVR was the most accurate model on RMSE, MAE and MAPE. ARIMAX came second on RMSE and MAPE, followed by LASSO and XGBoost, while the 1D-CNN and the Naive forecast came next and the Seasonal Naive forecast was the worst. The lead of SVR over ARIMAX was very small (about 0.3% on RMSE), and only SVR did better than ARIMAX. LASSO and XGBoost were close to ARIMAX but not better on RMSE, and the 1D-CNN was worse on RMSE and MAPE and slightly better on MAE. Because all models used the same prepared data, a well-specified ARIMAX gave most of the gain that the machine learning models gave. The differences between the top four models were also small compared with the size of the errors, and the test period had only 24 months. The ranking could therefore change in another period, and no formal test of the differences (such as the Diebold–Mariano test; Diebold and Mariano, 1995) was applied in this study.

This pattern agrees with the mixed evidence in the literature. Wong and La (2024) found that machine learning added value for a volatile tax line but not for a stable one. Larson and Overton (2024) concluded that how the data are prepared matters as much as the choice of model, and Akinrinola et al. (2024) reported that no single technique is best in every setting. Some studies also found that traditional or hybrid models stay competitive when data are limited (Jayanti et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2025). Agbenyega et al. (2022) found that machine learning models clearly beat ARIMA variants for customs revenue in Ghana, and Ofori et al. (2021) found that ARIMA with intervention beat the Holt method and the GRA's own forecasts for VAT. This study adds that, for Domestic VAT, SVR was slightly better than a well-specified ARIMAX, but the gain was small.

Three reasons probably explain why the gains were small. First, the sample was small: there were 155 training months and 15 predictors. Models that need more data, such as the 1D-CNN, overfitted quickly, and the XGBoost trees had little data to learn from. The kernel method (SVR) coped better with the small sample, which was what was expected at the proposal stage. Second, the predictors were only weakly related to the monthly change in VAT (Figure 4.7), so there was little extra for a flexible model to find. Third, the largest errors came from sudden jumps that none of the models could foresee. In practice, a one-month-ahead forecast with an expected error of about 9% can be used as a check on monthly collection targets and to flag months when collections look unusually low or high, but it cannot replace judgement.

### 4.6.3 Factors that Influence Domestic VAT Revenue {#s4-6-3 .unnumbered .unlisted}

This section answers Research Question 3 and meets Objective 3. The models agreed on the main drivers of the monthly change in VAT. These were past changes in VAT (VAT tended to fall back after a strong month), the previous month's change in economic activity (CIEA), the previous month's change in the exchange rate, and the calendar (the December peak and the same month last year). Inflation and the T-bill rate carried little weight. The data did not contain administrative variables, such as the rollout of e-VAT or changes in the tax rate, so their effects could not be measured. These results show association and not proof of cause.

The importance of economic activity agrees with the literature, which treats economic activity and consumption as the main determinants of the VAT base (Section 2.2.3). The positive link with the exchange rate fits the view that a weaker cedi can raise nominal VAT receipts, although the literature also warns that depreciation can erode purchasing power (Section 2.2.3). Inflation was expected to matter, because Ghana's high inflation is said to compress real incomes and the VAT base. Its small weight here may be because monthly inflation was very noisy (Figure 4.3), so it carried little information about the next month's VAT. Sihotang et al. (2025) used the exchange rate, inflation and economic growth to forecast VAT in Indonesia. In this study, the exchange rate and economic activity were useful, but inflation was not.

## 4.7 Chapter Summary {#s4-7 .unnumbered .unlisted}

The exploratory analysis showed a strong upward trend, a December peak and a few extreme months. SVR gave the most accurate forecasts on RMSE, MAE and MAPE, but its lead over ARIMAX was small. LASSO and XGBoost beat the Naive forecast but not ARIMAX, the 1D-CNN did no better than the Naive forecast on RMSE, and the Seasonal Naive forecast was the weakest. All models missed the jump in August 2024. Past VAT changes, economic activity, the exchange rate and the December effect were the main drivers.

# CHAPTER 5 `<w:r><w:br/></w:r>`{=openxml}`\\`{=latex} SUMMARY, CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS {#ch5 .unnumbered .unlisted}

## 5.1 Introduction {#s5-1 .unnumbered .unlisted}

This chapter summarises the study, states the conclusions, and gives recommendations and suggestions for further research.

## 5.2 Summary of the Study {#s5-2 .unnumbered .unlisted}

Domestic VAT is a major source of revenue for Ghana, but it is hard to forecast. In 2024, it fell 24.3% short of its target, although total tax revenue exceeded its target (Ghana Revenue Authority, 2024). The aim of this study was to apply and evaluate machine learning models for forecasting Domestic VAT revenue in Ghana and to compare them with conventional forecasting methods.

Monthly data from January 2010 to December 2025 were used. LASSO, SVR, XGBoost and a 1D-CNN were applied, and compared with Naive, Seasonal Naive and ARIMAX benchmarks. The models forecast the monthly change in log VAT from 15 predictors based on earlier months. They were tuned by rolling validation on data up to December 2023 and tested on the 24 months from January 2024 to December 2025, using RMSE, MAE and MAPE.

## 5.3 Summary of Findings {#s5-3 .unnumbered .unlisted}

The findings follow the three objectives of the study.

1. **Apply machine learning models to forecast Domestic VAT revenue (Objective 1).** LASSO, SVR, XGBoost and a 1D-CNN were applied successfully. On the test data, SVR had an RMSE of 201.40, LASSO 204.69, XGBoost 210.25 and the 1D-CNN 239.63 (GHS million). The MAPE of the four models was between 9.36% and 10.07%.

2. **Compare the machine learning models with the conventional benchmarks (Objective 2).** ARIMAX, with the same predictors, had an RMSE of 201.94, and the Naive and Seasonal Naive forecasts had RMSEs of 239.65 and 371.59. SVR was the best model on RMSE, MAE (145.59) and MAPE (9.36%), but its lead over ARIMAX was very small. LASSO and XGBoost beat the Naive forecast on RMSE but not ARIMAX. The 1D-CNN did no better than the Naive forecast on RMSE. SVR was therefore the most suitable model, with ARIMAX a close and simpler alternative.

3. **Identify the key factors that influence Domestic VAT revenue (Objective 3).** Past changes in VAT, the previous month's changes in economic activity (CIEA) and in the exchange rate, and the December effect were the main drivers. Inflation and the T-bill rate had little weight.

## 5.4 Conclusions {#s5-4 .unnumbered .unlisted}

The study concluded that:

1. Machine learning models could forecast monthly Domestic VAT in Ghana with a typical error of about 9% to 10%. This was a clear gain over the Naive forecast in RMSE (12% to 16%), but it was not a large gain over a well-specified ARIMAX model.

2. SVR was the most accurate model on all three measures, so machine learning could match and slightly improve on the conventional model. With only 179 monthly observations, the more complex models (XGBoost and the 1D-CNN) did not do better than the simpler ones.

3. No model could predict sudden jumps, such as the one in August 2024. These months accounted for much of the forecast error.

4. Recent changes in VAT, economic activity and the exchange rate, together with the December effect, were useful clues for forecasting the next month's VAT.

## 5.5 Recommendations {#s5-5 .unnumbered .unlisted}

For the Ghana Revenue Authority and the Ministry of Finance:

1. Use SVR together with ARIMAX to produce one-month-ahead forecasts of Domestic VAT. Use them alongside existing methods, and compare them with actual collections every month. ARIMAX is easier to explain, and SVR was slightly more accurate.

2. Record policy and administrative events, such as changes in the VAT rate, the rollout of e-VAT and large payment or refund delays. Large errors came from sudden jumps, and these records would help to explain them and, in time, to model them.

3. Re-estimate the models when new data arrive, at least once a year, and report more than one error measure.

4. Treat the forecasts as a guide and not as a replacement for judgement, especially in months with known policy changes.

## 5.6 Limitations of the Study {#s5-6 .unnumbered .unlisted}

1. The sample was small (155 training months and 24 test months), which limited what complex models could learn.

2. Only aggregated, monthly, macroeconomic data were used. Administrative variables and taxpayer-level data were not available.

3. Only one-step-ahead forecasts were studied. The models were estimated once and not updated during the test period.

4. The test period included a few extreme months, so the ranking of the closest models may change in another period. No formal test of the differences between models was applied.

5. The results apply to Ghana's Domestic VAT and may not carry over to other taxes or countries.

## 5.7 Suggestions for Further Research {#s5-7 .unnumbered .unlisted}

1. Apply a formal test, such as the Diebold–Mariano test, to check whether differences between models are real.

2. Study forecasts for several months ahead, and re-estimate the models as new data arrive.

3. Add administrative and policy variables, such as VAT rate changes and e-VAT, and variables for the three unusual months.

4. Try hybrid models, such as ARIMAX combined with SVR, and combinations of forecasts.

5. Test more flexible models, such as the LSTM, when more data are available, for example from taxpayer-level or sector-level records.
